transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Methylation risk prediction, for Thursday, November 26.
Let's turn to Methylation risk prediction, where both new papers ask which epigenetic age measure you should trust.

The first is a meta-analysis from the Murgatroyd lab in Molecular Psychiatry. It pools seventeen studies, about ten thousand nine hundred people, to compare how eight DNA methylation clocks relate to adverse childhood experiences.
The clocks did not behave alike. GrimAge and DunedinPACE showed the strongest and most consistent age acceleration, but only DunedinPACE held up across strata.
So the authors argue that clock choice matters in stress-related risk research. A study's result could partly reflect which clock it happened to pick.
One caution: the summary doesn't describe the strata or the populations, so we can't say much about ancestry or how much the included studies differed.
The second paper is a bioRxiv preprint from the Gladyshev lab. It introduces LongReadClock, a set of epigenetic clocks for individual blood cell types.
They don't sort cells. Instead they run long-read whole-genome sequencing on bulk blood, assign each read to a cell type in silico, and estimate age to within roughly three to six years.
And the cell-type age deviations carry different signals. Myeloid age was associated with blood pressure and heart rate, while NK-cell age was associated with asthma.
That pairs well with the meta-analysis. If bulk clocks disagree, a cell-resolved readout might be one way to work out why.
Still, it's a preprint, and the summary gives no cohort size or replication, so treat those associations as leads, not established risk markers.
The takeaway: methylation age isn't one number, and both the clock and the cell type you measure shape the risk signal you find.

papers.title: Epigenetic clocks and adverse childhood experiences: a meta-analysis
Measuring Cell Type Resolved Aging Through Long-Read Sequencing
